problem: The sentence is broken: "A mixed state has r Chapter 2.6." Words are missing, so the key statement (mixed states have vector length less than 1 and sit inside the sphere) never reaches the student.
fix: A pure state has |r| = 1 and sits on the surface of the sphere. A mixed state has |r| < 1 and sits inside the sphere; it is described by a density matrix rather than a single ket, and Chapter 2.6 covers that.

where: Section 1 and Exam traps (also Quiz Q2, Quiz Q3 answer)
problem: Exponentials are written without superscript in the running text: "r₀eiγ₀", "eiδ", "eiφsin(θ/2)", "eiα|ψ⟩", "eiπ sin(π/4)". A phone reader can misread e·i·γ₀ as a product of three symbols instead of e raised to iγ₀, and the formula block uses <sup> while the text does not, so the notation looks inconsistent.
fix: Use the same form everywhere: α = r₀e<sup>iγ₀</sup>, β = r₁e<sup>iγ₁</sup>, e<sup>iδ</sup>, e<sup>iφ</sup>sin(θ/2), e<sup>iα</sup>|ψ⟩, e<sup>iπ</sup>sin(π/4).

problem: The stated reason ("The two basis states must be orthogonal") does not by itself explain why the angle on the sphere is twice the Hilbert-space angle. Orthogonality is what makes the poles antipodal, but the doubling needs to be said: orthogonal states are 90° apart as state vectors yet 180° apart on the sphere.
fix: Orthogonal states sit at antipodal points, so an angle of π/2 between state vectors becomes an angle of π on the sphere. That doubling is why the amplitudes carry θ/2: at θ = π the |1⟩ amplitude is sin(π/2) = 1, whereas cos θ and sin θ would put |1⟩ at θ = π/2 and break the poles.

where: Section 3, formula 'where' line and the paragraph after it
problem: The symbol r is used both for the vector, r = (sinθ cosφ, sinθ sinφ, cosθ), and for its length, "Bloch vector length r = 1". Students can confuse the vector with the scalar length.
fix: Keep r for the vector and write the length as |r| throughout: "A pure state has |r| = 1 ... a mixed state has |r| < 1."
